draft.title: Turning the turbines
card: A turbine can be turned by a moving fluid. Wind and flowing water turn it directly. Tides, the rise and fall of the sea, also push water through turbines.
Other power stations boil water to make steam. The heat comes from burning coal, oil or gas, or from nuclear fission, the splitting of atoms. The steam pushes the turbine.
Burning coal, oil or gas releases carbon dioxide, which adds to climate change. Wind, water and tides release none while running. Fission releases none either.
Each source has its own costs. Wind turbines depend on the weather, dams and tidal barriers change habitats, and nuclear fission leaves radioactive waste that needs safe storage.
draft.remember: Turbines are turned by wind, water, tides or steam, and each source has different costs and emissions.

a.q: Which power source turns a turbine with steam made by the heat from splitting atoms?
a.why: Fission splits atoms and the heat boils water into steam that pushes the turbine. Gas also makes steam, but its heat comes from burning, not from splitting atoms.
a.clue: Look for the source where atoms are split.

b.q: A town on the Victorian coast compares two plans: a wind farm, and a gas power station that makes steam. Which statement about running them is correct?
opts: Gas releases carbon dioxide when burnt, but wind does not
Wind releases carbon dioxide when it turns the blades
Both release the same carbon dioxide while running
Gas releases none, as steam is only water
b.why: Burning gas releases carbon dioxide while the plant runs. Wind turns blades directly and releases none while running. The steam is only water, but the carbon dioxide comes from the burning that heats it.
b.clue: Which plan involves burning a fuel?

b.best: Gas releases carbon dioxide when burnt, but wind does not
